newsitem.title: PERU: Peru police step up pressure at rebel siege site.
newsitem.headline: Peru police step up pressure at rebel siege site.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages chanted their defiance on Friday as the government sent armoured cars rumbling past the occupied Japanese ambassador's house for the first time since the 38-day-old siege began.

Two armoured personnel carriers with special forces police aiming their rifles at the residence made two passes directly in front of the siege site as a helicopter flew overhead with an armed policeman in a harness riding on its skids.

In response, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels broadcast a revolutionary song for the second time and chants of "Long Live the Revolution" and "Long Live Freedom" could be heard from inside the residence. The rebels had broadcast the same song earlier as dawn broke.
After the vehicles passed, an unidentifed hostage, looking worried and tired, appeared briefly at a window.

The Russian-made Caspir vehicles, each with a heavy machine gun on top, appeared at the siege site on Wednesday but Friday was the first day they crossed police cordons and lines of journalists two blocks from the residence to enter the restricted zone in front of the house.

The new police manoeuvres followed a warning by President Alberto Fujimori, visiting La Paz in neighbouring Bolivia on Thursday, that he intended to wipe out the MRTA after the crisis. "We are looking for the total eradication of the group in the region," he told reporters during a brief visit with Bolivia's President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada.
Fujimori said he would not let up in his fight against the rebels. "There is no going back. There are still isolated groups ... this government is going to hunt them down."

Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro is among the captives, has built much of his popular support on an aggressive fight against the MRTA and the larger and bloodier Maoist Shining Path rebel group. Local analysts say his efforts have reduced the MRTA to less than 250 active members.

Fujimori's tone underlined police tactics over the last few days stepping up pressure on the rebels in the residence. On Thursday four carpenters escorted by police boarded up one of the compound's two entrances and a small hole in the wall used by service staff, leaving only the entrance used by Red Cross workers, mediators and freed captives.
Police helicopters have also flown over the residence several times but not, as on Friday, with an armed officer riding shotgun outside the craft.
The MRTA has responded to the government's latest moves on the Internet, slamming Fujimori as a "dictator" whose security forces were preparing to storm the residence.

In a communique carried on its web home page, it said police activities around the diplomatic compound were "provocations that seek a pretext to justify military intervention ... We ask for the families, the press, human rights organisations and national and international solidarity to help prevent this massacre we warn of."
The roughly 15 rebels in the house are armed with assault rifles and grenade launchers and have mined and booby-trapped the compound against possible attack.

Though both sides have said they were willing to sit down to discuss a peaceful end to the crisis, Fujimori has ruled out starting talks until the rebels drop their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
The rebels have said there is no point in talking unless that demand is on the agenda.
The MRTA originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17.

They freed most of them in what they called "goodwill gestures," keeping those they consider the best bargaining chips including two Peruvian government ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen, and diplomats and ambassadors from Bolivia and Japan.
